evidence.claim: The Census Bureau reported that the official poverty rate in 2022 was 11.5 percent, while the Supplemental Poverty Measure was 12.4 percent and the SPM child poverty rate more than doubled from 5.2 percent in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022.
evidence.title: Poverty in the United States: 2022
evidence.excerpt: The Census Bureau reported that the official poverty rate in 2022 was 11.5 percent, while the Supplemental Poverty Measure was 12.4 percent and the SPM child poverty rate more than doubled from 5.2 percent in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary household-income and poverty report with explicit 2022 estimates.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Broad 2022 economic outcome under Biden; not fully attributable because the report reflects taxes, transfers, and inflation dynamics beyond presidential control.
contrary_evidence: Other measures showed the labor market remained strong, so the deterioration was mainly inflation/transfer driven rather than mass job loss.

evidence.claim: Treasury said the FY 2022 deficit fell by $1.4 trillion, the largest one-year decrease in the Federal deficit in American history.
evidence.title: Joint Statement of Janet L. Yellen, Secretary of the Treasury, and Shalanda D. Young, Director of the Office of Management and Budget, on Budget Results for Fiscal Year 2022
evidence.excerpt: Treasury said the FY 2022 deficit fell by $1.4 trillion, the largest one-year decrease in the Federal deficit in American history.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official budget results statement with quantified fiscal outcome.
evidence.period_fit: Covers fiscal year 2022 during Biden's term.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Administration-level fiscal outcome under Biden, though much of the decline reflected pandemic relief rolling off.
contrary_evidence: A large part of the change came from the fading of COVID-era emergency spending rather than new restraint alone.

evidence.claim: The Tax Policy Center found the IRA's tax provisions were highly progressive, with taxes rising by $6,060 for households in the top 1 percent and by $41,580 for the top 0.1 percent in 2023.
evidence.title: The Inflation Reduction Act Primarily Impacts Top 1 Percent of Taxpayers
evidence.excerpt: The Tax Policy Center found the IRA's tax provisions were highly progressive, with taxes rising by $6,060 for households in the top 1 percent and by $41,580 for the top 0.1 percent in 2023.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Respected nonpartisan distributional analysis, but still a model-based estimate rather than observed outcomes.
evidence.period_fit: Legislation enacted in 2022 with modeled distributional effects.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct attribution to Biden-backed legislation signed in 2022; effects are modeled, not observed.
contrary_evidence: Distributional estimates do not prove realized welfare gains for all households.

evidence.claim: PWBM estimated that the Inflation Reduction Act would reduce non-interest cumulative deficits by $248 billion over the budget window and that its impact on inflation would be statistically indistinguishable from zero.
evidence.title: Inflation Reduction Act: Preliminary Estimates of Budgetary and Macroeconomic Effects
evidence.excerpt: PWBM estimated that the Inflation Reduction Act would reduce non-interest cumulative deficits by $248 billion over the budget window and that its impact on inflation would be statistically indistinguishable from zero.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Well-regarded model-based estimate, but still an ex ante simulation with uncertainty.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 legislative estimate of Biden-backed policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct legislative attribution to the Biden administration, but model uncertainty remains.
contrary_evidence: Model results differ from other estimates and do not guarantee realized inflation effects.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Biden told Powell he respected the independence of the Federal Reserve and would give the Fed space to fight inflation without political interference.
evidence.title: Biden vows to give Fed Chair Powell 'space' to fight inflation
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Biden told Powell he respected the independence of the Federal Reserve and would give the Fed space to fight inflation without political interference.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters is a strong contemporaneous news source; the claim is explicit but reported through a White House readout.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and squarely relevant to monetary credibility and macro management.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Biden behavior toward the Fed during his term.
contrary_evidence: This does not itself prove he never pressured the Fed in other ways, but it is direct evidence of restraint in this meeting.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that U.S. nonfarm payrolls increased by 528,000 in July 2022 and that employment rose above its pre-pandemic level while wages continued rising at a steady pace.
evidence.title: Instant View: US July payrolls rise more than expected
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that U.S. nonfarm payrolls increased by 528,000 in July 2022 and that employment rose above its pre-pandemic level while wages continued rising at a steady pace.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters report on the official jobs release; strong for outcome framing, though syndicated.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Macro outcome under Biden, but mainly an outcome claim rather than a direct presidential-action claim.
contrary_evidence: Strong employment does not by itself establish fair distribution or Biden-specific causation.

evidence.claim: Commerce said it was seeking information to design programs to incentivize investment in semiconductor manufacturing, shared infrastructure for research and prototyping, and related research, explicitly aiming to support a strong domestic semiconductor industry.
evidence.title: Commerce Department Requests Information on Supporting a Strong U.S. Semiconductor Industry
evidence.excerpt: Commerce said it was seeking information to design programs to incentivize investment in semiconductor manufacturing, shared infrastructure for research and prototyping, and related research, explicitly aiming to support a strong domestic semiconductor industry.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official administration implementation record with precise program-design language and date.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and part of Biden's industrial-policy agenda.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Biden-administration policy choice through Commerce.
contrary_evidence: The same document acknowledged immediate shortages and a long-term supply-chain vulnerability.

evidence.claim: Commerce announced CHIPS for America leadership and said the hires would have responsibility for implementing the CHIPS and Science Act's historic $50 billion semiconductor investment.
evidence.title: Biden-Harris Administration Announces CHIPS for America Leadership
evidence.excerpt: Commerce announced CHIPS for America leadership and said the hires would have responsibility for implementing the CHIPS and Science Act's historic $50 billion semiconductor investment.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official implementation announcement with named governance structure and responsibility.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 implementation of a Biden-backed industrial policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Biden-administration implementation under his authority.
contrary_evidence: Implementation setup does not by itself prove economic success or fair distribution.

evidence.claim: Brookings argued that infrastructure investment can stimulate economic growth and unleash job creation nationally, and that IIJA, IRA, and CHIPS together were sending hundreds of billions toward new projects and jobs.
evidence.title: Seizing the U.S. infrastructure opportunity: Investing in current and future workers
evidence.excerpt: Brookings argued that infrastructure investment can stimulate economic growth and unleash job creation nationally, and that IIJA, IRA, and CHIPS together were sending hundreds of billions toward new projects and jobs.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent policy analysis from a reputable think tank; still evaluative rather than observed outcome data.
evidence.period_fit: Late-2022 analysis of Biden-era legislation and its expected effects.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Policy package enacted under Biden, though future outcomes depend on implementation and labor-market conditions.
contrary_evidence: The same analysis warned that workforce shortages could limit gains if not addressed.

evidence.claim: Brookings said the IIJA offered an unprecedented opportunity to accelerate higher-wage careers and expand opportunities for workers, including the unemployed, underemployed, younger students, and adult learners.
evidence.title: Harnessing the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to train the next generation of workers
evidence.excerpt: Brookings said the IIJA offered an unprecedented opportunity to accelerate higher-wage careers and expand opportunities for workers, including the unemployed, underemployed, younger students, and adult learners.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent analysis that ties the law to workforce and wage opportunity, but remains prospective.
evidence.period_fit: 2022 law and its expected effects in the target period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly tied to Biden-backed enacted infrastructure policy.
contrary_evidence: The article frames this as an opportunity, not a guaranteed realized outcome.

evidence.claim: Treasury said the Inflation Reduction Act would make America more competitive, lower health and energy costs for families, create high-quality jobs, bolster energy security, sharply lower emissions, reduce the budget deficit, and increase long-term economic growth.
evidence.title: Statement by Secretary of the Treasury Janet L. Yellen on the Passage of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022
evidence.excerpt: Treasury said the Inflation Reduction Act would make America more competitive, lower health and energy costs for families, create high-quality jobs, bolster energy security, sharply lower emissions, reduce the budget deficit, and increase long-term economic growth.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official administration statement on the enacted law and its intended economic effects.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022, immediately after passage of a Biden-backed law.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Biden administration policy and signing-era agenda, though this is an intent/benefits statement rather than an outcome measure.
contrary_evidence: Official intent statements can overstate likely benefits; independent estimates are needed for calibration.

evidence.claim: The executive order described the IRA as the single largest and most ambitious investment in the U.S. ability to advance clean energy, cut consumer energy costs, promote environmental justice, strengthen energy security, reduce the deficit, and grow the economy.
evidence.title: Executive Order 14082—Implementation of the Energy and Infrastructure Provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022
evidence.excerpt: The executive order described the IRA as the single largest and most ambitious investment in the U.S. ability to advance clean energy, cut consumer energy costs, promote environmental justice, strengthen energy security, reduce the deficit, and grow the economy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary executive order text, though it is largely declarative and promissory in nature.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 presidential action implementing the IRA.
contrary_evidence: Implementation promises do not prove realized economic gains in 2022.

unresolved_gaps: Direct 2022 command-and-control and safeguards evidence is thinner than the public nuclear rhetoric and treaty-posture record.
The strongest crisis evidence is mostly speeches and reported private warnings rather than a declassified operational de-escalation record.
Direct 2022 documentary evidence on private diplomacy, ceasefire channels, and partner-use limits remains thinner than the public sanctions and aid record.
National-level evidence on protest policing, retaliation for dissent, and the federal government's leverage over local police remains thinner than the anti-hate and gun-safety record.
Border-enforcement attribution is still mixed because a large share of the harmful conduct sits in inherited systems and sub-agency action.
Direct evidence on state-level election administration, intimidation, and coercive presidential leverage against opponents is still limited.
Household distribution by race, region, and income tier is thinner than the macro and legislative record.
The causal split between Biden-era policy, global shocks, and Federal Reserve tightening remains mixed.
Child care, disability services, and elder-care evidence is still thin compared with health, housing, food, and crisis-response coverage.
The housing record is strong on funding and program design but weaker on realized rent-burden and eviction-prevention outcomes in 2022.
Direct personal-nexus evidence on recusal, ethics waivers, family-business benefit, or obstruction of scrutiny remains thin.
The clearest negative pattern is repeated factual exaggeration in speeches, but the record lacks equally direct correction or retraction evidence.
Independent project-level verification of 2022 execution for CHIPS, IRA, and infrastructure remains thinner than the policy-architecture record.
Community-level outcomes for specific groups and regions are still not well verified in the package.
